extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness of chemical compounds (genus/species, homologs, isomers, analogs) in patent examination, focusing on structural similarity, properties, predictability, and evidentiary burdens to establish or rebut a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Teachings of Structural Similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any teachings of a “typical,” “preferred,” or “optimum” species or subgenus within the disclosed genus. If such a prior art species or subgenus is structurally similar to that claimed, its disclosure may provide a reason for one of ordinary skill in the art to choose the claimed species or subgenus from the genus, based on the reasonable expectation that structurally similar species usually have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether prior art expressly teaches related species/subgenera or art-recognized equivalences (e.g., Merck v. Biocraft). Consider conservative substitutions in proteins and how substitution location affects function. The closer the physical/chemical similarities, the greater the expectation of equivalent function. Conversely, dissimilar disclosed species may teach away (cf. Baird). Preferred/optimum species that are structurally very different may weigh against selecting the claimed species. Consider cited cases (Dillon, Deuel, Jones, Susi) and use them as factual analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Number of Variables and Significance of Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: In making an obviousness determination, consider the number of variables which must be selected or modified, and the nature and significance of the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how many independent choices an ordinary artisan would have to make to arrive at the claimed species and whether differences are minor or substantive. Large differences or many variables (e.g., structural features absent in prior art) weigh against a prima facie case (see In re Jones, In re Susi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Teachings of Similar Properties or Uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the properties and utilities of the structurally similar prior art species or subgenus; properties and utilities provide real world motivation for selecting structurally similar species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention and structurally similar prior art share any useful property, that generally motivates an artisan to make the claimed species. Lack of known useful properties weighs against motivation. Prior art need not disclose newly discovered properties to support a prima facie case. Very close structural similarity may allow presuming similar properties (see Dillon, Stemniski, Grabiak, Wilder, Lintner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Predictability of the Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the predictability of the technology: unpredictable fields make it less likely that structural similarity alone renders a claimed species obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art is unpredictable, structural similarity is less persuasive because one cannot reasonably infer shared properties. Obviousness requires only a reasonable expectation of success, not certainty. Use relevant cases (May, Schechter, O’Farrell) to assess whether unpredictability in the field rebuts a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Any Other Teaching To Support the Selection of the Species or Subgenus
rubrics_metrics.description: The categories of relevant teachings (structural similarity, similar properties, predictability) are not exclusive; consider the totality of the evidence and any other relevant teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unusual cases there may be other teachings sufficient to support selection of the species or subgenus. Office personnel should evaluate all evidence on motivation, suggestion, or reason to combine/select, not just the most common categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Express Fact-Findings and Determine Whether They Support a Prima Facie Case of Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors, focusing primarily on the prior art teachings discussed above, and specifically articulate any teachings or suggestions that would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicit fact-findings and a rationale (as required by KSR) that ties prior art teachings to a conclusion of obviousness. Thereafter determine whether, considered as a whole, these findings establish a prima facie case that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Cite In re Bell, In re Kulling, Panduit for support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close Structural Similarity Between Chemical Compounds Can Support a Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities; motivation arises from expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this presumption cautiously: show how structural closeness and similar utilities would have motivated the skilled artisan (see In re Payne, In re Dillon, Papesch). Use prior case law to determine when similarity suffices to create a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology and Isomerism Must Be Considered with All Other Relevant Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Homologs and isomers are generally close structural similarities that create a presumed expectation of similar properties, but homology/isomerism alone does not automatically equate to prima facie obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the context of the disclosure as a whole. Homologs far removed from adjacent homologs or isomers that are not considered equivalent by skilled chemists may not support a prima facie case (see Wilder, May, Mills, Wiechert, Langer). Do not assume homology alone controls the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a True Homologous or Isomeric Relationship Is Not Controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art structures do not have to be true homologs or isomers to render structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious; non-homologous but structurally similar compounds can still motivate selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to overall structural and functional similarity and whether an ordinary artisan would be motivated to make the claimed compound even if it is not a strict homolog/isomer (see Payne, Mayne, Merck, Dillon). Conversely, also consider cases where substitution was not suggested (Grabiak, Bell, Deuel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or Absence of Prior Art Suggestion of a Method of Making the Claimed Compound May Be Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition of matter may affect whether that composition is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the relevant time, that may overcome a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity (see Maloney, Hoeksema, Payne). Consider whether a prior-art synthesis would have led an artisan to the claimed compound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Obviousness Is Overcome Where There Is No Reasonable Expectation of Similar Properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of obviousness based on a reference disclosing structurally similar compounds may be overcome where evidence shows there is no reasonable expectation of similar properties in structurally similar compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence demonstrating unpredictability or contrary properties that rebut the expectation (see May, Schechter, Ex parte Blattner). Use experimental, factual, or authoritative evidence to show lack of reasonable expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If Prior Art Compounds Have No Utility, or Utility Only as Intermediates, They May Not Render Structurally Similar Compounds Prima Facie Obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious in the absence of reason to make the reference compounds or related compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prior art compounds were disclosed as useful or merely intermediates. Prior art teaching of no useful property or only intermediate use undermines motivation to make related compounds (see Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Facie Case Rebuttable by Evidence of Unexpected Results
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit or other evidence showing unexpectedly different utility/performance can overcome obviousness (see Papesch, Wiechert). However, mere recognition of a benefit by applicant is insufficient if the prior art compound actually possessed the benefit even if unrecognized (Dillon). Consult MPEP § 716.02–§ 716.02(g) for evidence types and handling.
